title: Dependable Inference for Product Teams — Brief
content:
Purpose:
This one-page brief crystallizes a product-facing positioning for Redwood that centers on predictable, dependable inference as a strategic advantage for product teams. It is aimed at product leads, engineering managers, and platform owners evaluating LLM strategy and vendor trade-offs.

Core problem we solve:
- Building LLM features in production is brittle: cost surprises, intermittent latency spikes, and silent quality regressions force product teams to choose between slow iteration and risky launches.
- Many vendors sell models or raw infrastructure; customers need service guarantees that map directly to product outcomes (latency, cost per active user, error budgets, and predictable rollouts).

Positioning statement (single sentence):
For product teams that treat user experience as the primary metric, Redwood is the inference platform that makes LLM features predictable and operable at scale — lowering cost and risk while letting teams iterate fast.

Thesis (2–3 paragraphs):
As models proliferate, competitive advantage shifts from having the best model to reliably delivering the experience the model enables. Product teams don’t win by trading up models; they win by shipping consistent, resilient experiences. That requires inference built as a product: SLOs for latency and quality, meaningful cost controls that map to unit economics, and operational primitives (rollouts, fallbacks, observability) that let teams iterate safely.

Redwood is designed around those primitives. We treat serving as a first-class product layer — not a dataset, not a model catalog. That means automated prefix caching and batching to control tail-latency, deterministic fallbacks to cheaper model variants when constraints tighten, and integrated quality monitors that guard against regressions tied to customer prompt sets. Those capabilities shrink time-to-value and make performance predictable as usage scales.

Why this matters to product leads (key benefits):
- Faster, safer launches: built-in canary and rollback mechanics mean new LLM features can be rolled out incrementally without full rework.
- Predictable unit economics: per-route cost telemetry and Optimize recommendations let PMs forecast costs per DAU or per-call.
- User-facing reliability: latency SLOs and region-aware routing keep latency consistent across geographies.
- Reduced operational burden: platform teams get a unified API and runbook-friendly fallbacks rather than bespoke model glue.

Key differentiators (how to articulate simply):
- Serving-first design: We optimize for production curves — latency vs. cost vs. quality — instead of maximizing model-only benchmarks.
- Operational primitives for product outcomes: canaries, A/B rollouts, fallback policies, and per-prompt regression alerts are standard, not add-ons.
- Unified experience across deployment modes: same API and tooling whether you use Hosted, Dedicated, or Private.
- Cost-aware inference controls: actionable batching, caching, and quantization suggestions that translate into real per-user savings.

Competitive takeaways (concise notes for sales):
- Against managed model endpoints: competitors sell GPUs + access; Redwood sells predictable outcomes. Emphasize SLOs, fallbacks, and unit economics.
- Against hosted-only LLM APIs: highlight private and dedicated options for regulated customers plus the same developer surface.
- Against self-hosted runtimes: we offer runtime performance tuned for production plus orchestration and observability — less ops work for the same latency.

Proof points & evidence to surface (examples to include in pitches):
- Case example: messaging app reduced avg token cost by 42% using prefix caching + batching while keeping 95th percentile latency within target through smart routing. (Internal study: Optimize-eval Q2 2025.)
- Benchmarks: 99th percentile latency profiles for typical chat workloads across Hosted vs. Dedicated with quantization variants.
- Product metrics: rollout success rate, time-to-rollback, and alert-to-resolution mean times as supporting operational metrics.

Core messaging bullets for website/one-pager (short):
- Ship LLM features that behave like first-class product features — predictable latency, predictable cost, predictable quality.
- Built-in rollouts and fallbacks so you can iterate quickly without outages.
- Unified runtime for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Objection handling (short scripts):
- "We can host ourselves and save money." -> "Self-hosting hides the operational cost of unpredictable tails. Redwood pays down that risk with deterministic behaviors and tooling that reduces your SRE and platform overhead; many teams find the all-in cost lower when you include incident load and engineering time."
- "We need full control for compliance." -> "Redwood Private offers the same serving primitives in a VPC or on-prem deployment, plus audit logs and KMS integrations — same API, same rollouts."

Quick pitch (30–45 seconds):
Most LLM problems aren’t model selection — they’re shipping reliably. Redwood gives product teams the primitives they need to make inference a predictable product: latency and quality SLOs, cost telemetry that ties to unit economics, and rollout/fallback tools that let you iterate safely. The net result is faster launches, fewer incidents, and clearer cost forecasts.

Suggested collateral and experiments to build next (tactical):
- One-pager: ‘Cost Per Active User’ calculator showing how Optimize suggestions reduce per-DAU costs.
- Demo script: incremental rollout of a summarization feature showing canary, failure injection, and automated fallback.
- Sales playbook: objections + customer evidence matrix for regulated industries and platform teams.

Open questions / decisions (notes to GTM):
- Which short-form customer evidence stories are highest priority for the site? (billing + latency wins vs. reliability/incident reduction)
- Standardize a small set of benchmark workloads to reference in public collateral.
- Map pricing experiments to the ‘per-active-user’ narrative so PMs can evaluate economics quickly.

Author notes (for internal editors):
- Keep language product-focused; avoid deep runtime jargon in outward-facing copy. Use the runtime specifics only in technical sell or datasheets.
- This brief is intended to complement engineering-focused collateral (which should retain kernel/quantization depth) and customer case studies (which will validate numbers).

End of brief.
